mainEntity.name: Is it a dental emergency if my crown comes off?

acceptedAnswer.text: A dislodged crown is not always classified as a dental emergency, but it does require timely professional attention. If you are experiencing significant pain, swelling, or signs of infection, it is advisable to contact your dental practice promptly or seek urgent dental care. If you have no discomfort and the underlying tooth appears undamaged, your practice may still aim to see you within a short period to assess the situation and protect the exposed tooth from further risk.

mainEntity.name: Can I re-cement my crown at home?

acceptedAnswer.text: Temporary dental adhesive products are available from pharmacies and can provide short-term comfort, but they are not designed to serve as a permanent solution. Attempting to permanently re-cement a crown at home is not advisable, as doing so without assessing the underlying tooth could mask decay, damage the tooth further, or result in a poor fit. Always seek a professional assessment to determine the most appropriate course of action for your individual circumstances.

mainEntity.name: How long can I leave a crown off before seeing a dentist?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is generally advisable to contact your dental practice as soon as possible rather than waiting. The longer the underlying tooth remains exposed, the greater the risk of sensitivity, contamination, or further damage. Whilst the urgency will depend on your symptoms and the condition of the tooth, most dental professionals recommend seeking assessment within a day or two of the crown coming off, wherever possible.

mainEntity.name: Why did my crown come off in the first place?

acceptedAnswer.text: There are several possible reasons a crown may come off, including natural deterioration of the dental cement over time, decay developing beneath the crown, physical force such as biting hard foods or grinding teeth, or changes in the fit of the crown due to alterations in the tooth structure. Your dentist will assess the specific circumstances during your appointment and explain the findings of their examination.

mainEntity.name: Will I need a completely new crown?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not necessarily. Whether the existing crown can be re-cemented or whether a new one is required depends on the condition of the crown itself and the state of the underlying tooth. If the crown is intact and the tooth is in good condition, re-cementing may be suitable. If there is damage, decay, or a significant change in fit, a new crown may be recommended. This can only be determined following a clinical assessment.

mainEntity.name: Does a tooth still need a crown if the nerve has already been treated?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. A tooth that has undergone root canal treatment often becomes more brittle over time and benefits from the protection of a crown. The crown helps to maintain the structural integrity of the tooth and prevent fracture. If the crown on a root canal-treated tooth comes off, it is particularly important to seek assessment promptly, as the tooth may be at greater risk without the protective restoration in place.
